All soils are dry for this work, with a water table below the depth of the pipe. Table 1 shows the failure pressures in psi for each of the six pipeline cases using the expressions from section 2. Note that the table includes two pressures for cross-section buckling for the first and third cases; these are the two buried cases, and hence there are two equations to assess. In case 1, equation 1 provides the lower pressure, while in case 3 the second equation provides the lower number. Representative Nuclear Weapon Pressures Compared to Collapse Pressures To assess how these pressure limits correlate to pressures prevalent in nuclear weapon detonations, we can use source [8] to provide estimates for a 1 kT ground burst, which can then be scaled to higher yields (in this case to 10, 100, and 1000 kT). Table 2 shows distance ground range from source where pressures meet or exceed 2000 and 500 psi for overpressures and 50 and 15 psi for dynamic pressure. Table 2. From Table 2, we see that a 100 kT blast would collapse all of these within at least 557 feet from ground zero, where the overpressure is at least 2000 psi. Cases 5 and 6 require overpressures in excess of 3200 psi, and so would only collapse much closer to ground zero. However, these are more susceptible to longitudinal buckling. Case 5 needs only a dynamic pressure of 12 psi, which from Table 2 is shown to be achieved within at least 2785 feet from ground zero. In general, these calculations indicate that above ground pipes with wide support spacings are most susceptible to longitudinal buckling. A complication to these considerations is that the values provided for overpressures and dynamics pressures are peak values which then decay in time, whereas structural collapse calculations generally 13 assume an applied constant force.
